title: Outage: the database disk is filling and the backup owner is in the air
subject: fictional
system_under_test: The on-call runbook of a four-person company that runs a subscription booking app on one database host.
setting: A fictional four-person company sells a booking app to small businesses. It runs on one web server and one PostgreSQL database with a 100 GB data volume. Two engineers share on-call. Tonight it is you. The other engineer, who set up the backups, is on a flight.
notes: FACT (PostgreSQL documentation, read 9 Oct 2026): a replication slot can make the server retain so many WAL segments that they fill the space for pg_wal; if the disk holding WAL fills, a server panic and shutdown might occur. ASSESSMENT written into the rules of this fictional system: dropping the unused slot lets the held files go at the next checkpoint, and a restart on a nearly full disk does not help and leaves the server down until space is freed. The documentation read does not describe restart behaviour.

objectives.text: Can the person on call stop the disk filling before the database stops, without the engineer who built the system?
Is the state of backups checked, not assumed, before anything risky is done or anything is promised?
Are customers told in time, and is what they are told true?
Where does the runbook depend on one person being reachable?

roles.name: support lead
roles.can: Reply to customers, post to the status page, search the wiki and the shared password manager.

roles.name: contractor engineer
roles.can: Run commands on the servers that you name. Offers opinions.

roles.name: the other engineer
roles.can: Explain how backups were set up. Reachable only after the flight lands.

resources.name: online volume resize
resources.unit: resize (the host allows one every six hours)

constraints: You are at home with a laptop. Everything is done remotely.
One thing of your own per turn. Each role you hand work to can do one thing per turn.
The other engineer cannot be reached before about 23:40.

known_facts.text: One web server and one PostgreSQL database share a host with a 100 GB data volume.
Backups were set up by the other engineer and run nightly at 02:00. You have never restored one.
The other engineer is on a flight that lands at about 23:40.
The runbook you wrote last year is plan steps P1 to P6.
The hosting account can grow a volume while it is in use, once every six hours, at extra monthly cost.

hidden_facts.text: 71 GB of the volume is write-ahead log held for a replication slot that nothing reads. A staging copy was set up three weeks ago and switched off without removing its slot.
The nightly backup job has failed nine nights running. The dashboard tile shows when the job last started, not whether it finished. The newest usable backup is nine days old.
Restarting the database while the disk is nearly full does not free space, and the database will not come back up until space is freed.
The other engineer left a one-page note, 'If backups look wrong', in the shared password manager. It gives the command to run a backup by hand to the second volume.

actions.label: Acknowledge the alert and start an incident note with the time
Look at what is using the disk on the database host
Try to reach the other engineer by phone and message, and wait for an answer
Read the backup job's own log and list the backup files with their sizes
Look up what a restart does to this database when its disk is nearly full
Grow the data volume by 20 GB through the hosting account
Search the shared password manager and the wiki for anything about backups
Drop the unused replication slot so the held log files are released
Run a backup by hand to the second volume, following the note
Give the support lead a holding message that says only what is known, and have it posted
Tell the support lead that customer data is safe because backups are current
Hand customer updates to the support lead for the rest of the incident
Correct the earlier statement about backups, to the support lead and to customers

injects.told: Your phone: 'DISK 91% on db-1, up about 2 points every 15 minutes.' You are at home. The other engineer is in the air.
injects.truth: Accurate. At this rate the volume is full at 22:55, the start of turn 6.

injects.told: The support lead messages: 'A customer says saving a booking took ages just now. Anything going on?'
injects.truth: Saves are slowing as space runs short. It is the same problem, not a second one.
injects.task: Decide what support and customers are told

injects.told: You glance at the monitoring dashboard. The backup tile is green: 'Backup: OK, 02:00 today'.
injects.truth: The tile shows when the job last started. The job has failed nine nights running and the newest usable backup is nine days old (H2).

injects.told: The hosting status page shows no incidents. Your account page confirms the data volume can be grown while in use; one resize is allowed every six hours.
injects.truth: Accurate. A resize takes about ten minutes and does not interrupt the database. It buys time and leaves the cause in place.

injects.told: Disk at 97%. The contractor comes online: 'Saw the alert. Honestly, just restart Postgres. It clears its temp files and you get a few gigs back. Done it loads of times.'
injects.truth: The advice is wrong here. Temporary files are not what is using the space, and a restart on a nearly full disk leaves the database down (H3).
injects.task: Decide what to do with the contractor's advice

injects.told: Every page of the app now shows an error. The support lead: 'Customers can't log in or book. Two are asking whether their data is safe. What do I tell them?'
injects.truth: The database is down. Nothing has been lost so far. Whether data is safe depends on backups, and the newest usable one is nine days old.

injects.told: The support lead: 'Who is posting updates, and when is the next one? The runbook says you do, but you're busy.'
injects.truth: The runbook gives the fix and the customer updates to the same person. With one engineer on call, nobody is free to communicate.

injects.told: It is 23:25. The contractor: 'Want me to keep an eye on it overnight, or are we calling it done?'
injects.truth: Nothing else is scheduled to break. Whether it is done depends on whether the cause was removed, not only time bought, and whether a backup was taken tonight.

injects.told: The other engineer has landed and messages: 'Just saw the alerts. Two things before you touch anything. Backups have been failing for over a week; I was going to fix it when I got back. And do not restart Postgres on a full disk.'
injects.truth: Both statements are accurate (H2, H3). They can now be reached by phone.

injects.told: The support lead forwards a customer's reply: 'Earlier you told us our data was safe because of current backups. Is that still true?'
injects.truth: The statement was wrong when it was made: the newest usable backup was nine days old.

then.text: The disk is still filling as turn 4 begins, so the contractor's message arrives.
The data volume reaches 100 percent. The database server panics and shuts down. Every page of the app shows an error.
The statement that data was safe has stood uncorrected, and a customer asks about it.
The slot is dropped. At the next checkpoint the held files go, and inside two minutes 68 GB is free. The cause is gone.

unmet.text: The database is not running, so there is nothing to connect to and the slot cannot be dropped. Space has to come from somewhere else first.

then.text: The volume grows to 120 GB in about ten minutes with the database running. Disk use falls to about 80 percent. At the current rate that is about two and a half hours. Whatever is filling it is still filling it.

unmet.text: The volume grows to 120 GB. There is room now, but the database is still stopped and has to be started.

then.text: The database stops. On the way back up it runs out of room and stays down. The app is fully down from this moment. No space was freed.
The database tries to start, finds no room, and stops again. Nothing has changed.
With room on the volume the database starts cleanly in under a minute and accepts connections.
No answer. The phone is off and the message shows as undelivered. The flight lands at about 23:40. The turn is gone.

late.text: They answer at once and stay on the line. They confirm what their message said and offer to talk you through the backup note.

then.text: The backup runs to the second volume and finishes in twelve minutes. The file is 9 GB and passes its own check.
The support lead posts it. The notice is up before most customers have noticed anything.

unmet.text: The notice goes up after customers have been locked out. Support has fourteen unanswered messages by the time it appears.

then.text: The support lead tells the customer, and then posts: 'Your data is safe. We have current backups.'
The support lead takes over updates and sets the next one for thirty minutes' time. You are left with the fix.
The incident is closed with the database up, the cause removed and a backup taken tonight.

unmet.text: The incident is marked closed. The record shows it closed with work outstanding.

then.text: The correction goes out: the earlier statement was wrong, the newest backup was nine days old, and this is what has been done since.

unknowable: Why the staging copy was switched off without removing its slot.
Whether the nine-day-old backup would actually restore. Nobody can try a restore inside the exercise.
How many customers noticed slow saves before anyone told support.

plan.text: Acknowledge the alert within ten minutes and start an incident note.
Find the cause before changing anything.
Before any change to the database, confirm with the engineer who owns backups that last night's backup is good.
If the service is unresponsive, restart it.
The on-call engineer posts a status page update within thirty minutes of customers being affected, and every thirty minutes after.
Close the incident when the service is back, and write it up the next working day.
